subject: psychology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Von Frisch's research on honeybees showed they communicate the location of food using what?
questions.explain: Von Frisch found bees use a waggle dance to signal the direction and distance of food sources.

questions.q: Research suggesting the Inuit have many words for snow is used to discuss which hypothesis?
questions.explain: The 'words for snow' example is often cited (and debated) in relation to the Sapir-Whorf linguistic relativity hypothesis.

questions.q: The study by Carmichael showing labels changed how people redrew shapes supports which idea?
options: That language can influence memory and thought
questions.explain: Carmichael found that verbal labels biased how figures were reproduced, supporting language's influence on thought.

questions.q: Which of the following is a form of NON-VERBAL communication?
questions.explain: Body language is non-verbal communication, conveying meaning without words.

questions.q: The 'nature' side of the language debate is best supported by which idea?
options: Children only copy adults word for word
Language is learned solely through reward
Humans have an innate language acquisition device
questions.explain: The nature view is supported by Chomsky's idea of an innate language acquisition device present from birth.

questions.q: Which feature is generally UNIQUE to human language compared with animal communication?
questions.explain: Displacement, the ability to refer to things distant in time or space, is a hallmark of human language.

questions.q: Standing very close to someone who wants more space is an example of breaking which non-verbal norm?
questions.explain: Standing too close violates personal-space norms, a key aspect of non-verbal communication.

questions.q: A key difference between human language and animal communication is that human language is what?
questions.explain: Human language is productive and generative, allowing endless novel sentences, unlike most animal systems.

questions.q: The 'nurture' side of the language debate argues that language is mainly acquired through what?
questions.explain: The nurture view holds that language is learned through imitation, reinforcement and environmental input.

questions.q: Vygotsky believed that language and thought develop in what way?
options: They start separately then merge, with language shaping thought
questions.explain: Vygotsky argued language and thought begin separately and merge, with social language driving cognitive development.

questions.q: The nativist view (e.g. Chomsky) suggests humans are born with what?
questions.explain: Nativists argue humans have an innate, biological capacity that makes language acquisition possible.

questions.q: 'Personal space' in non-verbal communication refers to what?
options: The distance we keep between ourselves and others
questions.explain: Personal space is the comfortable physical distance people keep between themselves and others.

questions.q: Open, relaxed posture compared with crossed arms is an example of communication through what?
questions.explain: Posture is part of body language, a form of non-verbal communication that signals attitude and mood.

questions.q: Critics of the strong Sapir-Whorf hypothesis argue that people can do what?
options: Think about concepts even without a word for them
questions.explain: A key criticism is that people can grasp concepts they have no specific word for, weakening linguistic determinism.

questions.q: Which is a recognised FUNCTION of language?
questions.explain: A core function of language is to communicate ideas, information and intentions between people.

questions.q: Reduced eye contact in conversation can communicate what?
options: Things such as discomfort or dishonesty
questions.explain: Eye contact is a non-verbal signal; reduced eye contact may signal discomfort, shyness or evasiveness.

questions.q: Maintaining appropriate eye contact during conversation typically serves which function?
questions.explain: Eye contact helps regulate the flow of conversation and signals interest and attention to the other person.

questions.q: A strong limitation of von Frisch's bee 'waggle dance' as language is that it lacks what?
options: Productivity and the ability to discuss new topics
questions.explain: The waggle dance is fixed and limited, lacking the productivity and flexibility of true human language.

questions.q: Tone of voice (paralanguage) is best classed as which kind of communication?
questions.explain: Tone of voice, or paralanguage, is non-verbal because it conveys meaning beyond the words themselves.

questions.q: The Sapir-Whorf hypothesis (linguistic relativity) claims what?
options: Thought has no link to language
Language influences the way we think
questions.explain: The Sapir-Whorf hypothesis proposes that the language we speak shapes and influences how we think.

questions.q: Piaget's view on language and thought is that what comes first?
questions.explain: Piaget argued that thought develops first and language reflects a child's existing level of thinking.

questions.q: A key contrast between Piaget and Vygotsky is that Vygotsky placed more emphasis on what?
options: Social interaction and culture in language development
questions.explain: Vygotsky stressed the role of social interaction and culture, whereas Piaget focused on individual cognitive stages.
